text:
The passages suggest two complementary approaches:

- **Make forecasts quantitative and subject to accuracy feedback.** Explicit probability estimates can be objectively scored over time, providing feedback that enables learning. Falsifiable “signposts” can reveal whether events support a scenario, while comparison with aggregate forecasts provides a check on individual judgments. (https://intelligence.org/2013/05/01/agi-impacts-experts-and-friendly-ai-experts/)
- **Reward understanding other people’s views.** “Reciprocal scoring” gives higher scores to forecasters who accurately predict other experts’ and forecasters’ predictions. (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/K2xQrrXn5ZSgtntuT/what-do-xpt-forecasts-tell-us-about-ai-risk-1) The proposed reason to take such understanding seriously is that someone who can accurately predict your beliefs yet still disagrees apparently understands your model and may know something you do not—making their rival view worth hearing rather than dismissing. (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/cLtdcxu9E4noRSons/part-1-amplifying-generalist-research-via-forecasting-models)

These are not established guarantees: the passages explicitly note insufficient evidence that reciprocal-scoring accuracy predicts long-range forecasting accuracy. (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/K2xQrrXn5ZSgtntuT/what-do-xpt-forecasts-tell-us-about-ai-risk-1)
